findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: Council's housing development plans revised downward by £4.222m
findings.detail: New build and acquisition schemes have been reprofiled downward by £4.222m to reflect a revised housing growth programme, suggesting the council has reduced its planned housing development output.
findings.matters: Reductions to housing development plans can indicate demand softness or financial constraints. Changes to growth investment plans are material to understanding a council's future position.
findings.figures: £4.222m slippage on new build and acquisitions
findings.quote: Slippage of £4.222m on new build / acquisitions due to reprofiling of schemes to reflect revised housing growth programme.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: Gateshead Flyover project requires £12.289m additional funding due to work complexity
findings.detail: The major flyover demolition project's budget has increased from £11.725m to £24.014m — an increase of £12.289m. The council attributes this to project complexity and slippage from 2025/26, with completion still expected in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Significant cost overruns on major projects signal delivery challenges and require additional borrowing, indicating capital cost control issues.
findings.figures: Original £11.725m, revised £24.014m, additional funding £12.289m
findings.quote: The flyover is progressing well but due to the complexity of the works involved there was slippage in delivery from 2025/26 and it is expected to be completed during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - A
findings.headline: HRA capital delivery under internal service review with major programme deferrals
findings.detail: The council has initiated a service review of HRA (Housing Revenue Account) capital delivery and is deferring major housing schemes whilst assessing alternative delivery methods. Decent Homes has been cut by £8.978m and demolition/regeneration spend deferred by £9.635m, contributing to a total HRA capital reduction of £23.4m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council's ability to execute its capital programme as planned is fundamental to lender confidence. An active service review of housing delivery indicates operational uncertainty in a major capital spending area.
findings.figures: £23.454m HRA variance, £8.978m Decent Homes reduction, £9.635m demolition deferral
findings.quote: HRA capital delivery is currently subject to an internal service review. While alternative delivery methods are being assessed several housing schemes have been deferred, including Decent Homes (£8.978m variance). £9.635m of the variance relates to demolition spend that has been deferred into the following year.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A
findings.headline: Multiple capital schemes dependent on grant funding agreement with North East Mayoral Strategic Authority, creating delivery risk
findings.detail: Two major schemes—Gateshead Quays (£2.0m underspend) and Old Town Hall Quarter (£457k underspend)—were delayed specifically because the council was waiting for grant funding agreements to be finalised with the Mayoral Authority. This external dependency has added uncertainty to delivery timelines.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on whether capital programmes are under the council's control or dependent on third-party decision-making. Reliance on Mayoral Authority approvals for major schemes introduces governance risk beyond the council's direct management.
findings.figures: Gateshead Quays £2.0m variance, Old Town Hall Quarter £457k variance
findings.quote: Complex scheme resulting in additional time to finalise the grant funding agreement with the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A
findings.headline: District Energy Scheme (Old Fold/Nest House) paused due to viability concerns
findings.detail: A scheme to extend the Gateshead District Energy Network to the Old Fold/Nest estate, originally budgeted at £8.7m, was paused with only £616k spent. The council explicitly states the reason as 'viability issues', indicating the project economics or customer commitment did not stack up.
findings.matters: A lender funding energy transition or infrastructure work needs to understand why schemes fail viability tests. A £8.7m project paused mid-year suggests the council either miscalculated the business case or market conditions changed materially.
findings.figures: £8.669m original budget, £616k outturn, project paused
findings.quote: Project paused due to viability issues

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A
findings.headline: HRA Decent Homes programme scope under review following £3.9m underspend
findings.detail: The council's Decent Homes improvement programme, a substantial £8.1m commitment at Q3, delivered only £4.2m with the commentary noting that 'delivery and scope of works is currently under review'. This suggests uncertainty about what the council will actually deliver to its housing stock.
findings.matters: The HRA's asset management and maintenance strategy depends on reliable capital delivery. Scope uncertainty on this scale indicates planning or delivery challenges that could affect longer-term housing condition and viability.
findings.figures: £8.076m Q3 budget, £4.224m outturn, £3.9m variance
findings.quote: The delivery and scope of works is currently under review.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Capital Programme and Prudential Indicators – Year End Outturn 2025-26 - A
findings.headline: Gateshead Flyover demolition delayed by contract negotiation complexity, £11.9m underspend against Q3 budget
findings.detail: The flyover demolition was originally budgeted at £18.0m and only £6.1m was spent. The council attributes the delay to contract negotiation complexity. This is the single largest variance in the capital programme and indicates significant project delivery challenges on a major infrastructure scheme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether major infrastructure commitments are progressing on schedule, and persistent delays suggest either project management issues or unforeseen technical complexity that could affect the council's strategic capital plans and delivery capability.
findings.figures: £18.0m original budget, £6.124m outturn, £11.9m variance
findings.quote: Delays in contract negotiation due to the complexity of the works involved in removing the flyover.

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Report 25-26 Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: General Fund Capital Financing Requirement increased by £10.401m to £419.206m, signalling expanding capital commitments
findings.detail: The underlying need to borrow for capital spending grew significantly in one year, reflecting ongoing capital expenditure commitments. Total council CFR reached £764.711m, up from £754.310m. No breakdown is given of the capital projects driving this growth.
findings.matters: Growing capital commitments drive future external borrowing needs. Combined with the current internal borrowing position, this creates timing pressure for refinancing when investment balances run lower.
findings.quote: The Council's underlying need to borrow for capital expenditure and long-term liabilities is termed the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR).

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Report 25-26 Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: Council using £94.529m of internal borrowing to defer external borrowing, creating unspecified refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council deliberately used investment balances to fund capital spending rather than borrowing externally, saving on immediate costs but deferring refinancing of this internal borrowing to a future date when rates are expected to be lower. The document does not specify when this refinancing is planned or at what cost.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the refinancing timeline and cost for this significant liquidity commitment, as it represents a future borrowing need that could be substantial if capital programmes accelerate or investment balances tighten.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £94.529m at 31 March 2026 (General Fund £57.916m, HRA £36.613m)
findings.quote: the Council has continued to use investment balances to temporarily fund the capital programme. This has delivered a saving on borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Council is under-borrowed relative to liability benchmark and acknowledges need for external borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The liability benchmark calculation shows external debt is below the optimal level. Council explicitly acknowledges this under-borrowed position indicates future external borrowing will be required this year to align with the benchmark.
findings.matters: Under-borrowed position confirms financing gap that must be closed; affects the timing and cost of capital programme execution.
findings.figures: Borrowing requirement: General Fund £39.000m (vs estimate £43.116m), HRA £19.712m (vs estimate £34.712m)
findings.quote: external debt is below the benchmark and shows that we are in an under-borrowed position in 2026/27, indicating that we will need to take some external borrowing this year.

findings.headline: No borrowing taken in Q1 2026/27 as PWLB rates remain above budget at 5.71%
findings.detail: Council has taken zero new borrowing to date in 2026/27. Treasury is actively monitoring rates and deliberately holding off borrowing to avoid taking long-term loans at current elevated PWLB rates of 5.71%. Borrowing timing will depend on cash flow requirements for the capital programme.
findings.matters: Deferral of borrowing creates timing risk for capital programme financing; higher rates when borrowing does occur will increase long-term debt service costs.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing rates 5.71% at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Due to the current high long-term borrowing rates there has been no borrowing taken in the year to date. The timing of any further borrowing will depend on cash flow requirements to support the Capital Programme, pending the tracking of borrowing rates.

findings.headline: Investment income projection is 63% of budget due to lower cash balances from borrowing delay strategy
findings.detail: Gross investment income projected at £1.539m against budget of £2.450m. The variance of £0.739m is specifically attributed to the council's strategy of delaying borrowing, which has kept investment balances lower than estimated. This directly reduces revenue-side cash generation.
findings.matters: Lower cash generation from investments constrains available liquidity; signals council is intentionally running down cash balances while waiting for better borrowing rates.
findings.figures: £1.539m projected vs £2.450m budgeted; £0.739m variance
findings.quote: The £0.739m variance to budget is due to the strategy of delaying borrowing meaning investment balances are lower than estimated.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - NK
findings.headline: Adult social care demand pressures from care packages and children's transitions remain uncontrolled despite budget headroom
findings.detail: Adult Social Care shows £0 variance to its £102.9m budget, but the paper explicitly names continuing "demand-led pressures associated with care packages, including transitions from Children's Services." These are being absorbed within budget now but are described as ongoing structural issues.
findings.matters: Persistent demand pressures in adult social care that are managed in-year but not resolved signal future vulnerability. If these pressures are growing year-on-year, future budgets will face tighter margins and less room to absorb shocks elsewhere.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care budget £102.905m showing £0 variance despite stated structural pressures
findings.quote: Within Adult Social Care, demand-led pressures associated with care packages, including transitions from Children's Services continue to impact the cost base.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - NK
findings.headline: HRA reserve falling £1.058m to £5.388m with unresolved pressures in void loss and maintenance
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is balanced in-year only after drawing £1.058m from reserves. The paper identifies "underlying pressures within the HRA, particularly in relation to Void Loss and Repairs and Maintenance" with mitigation plans "being developed" — meaning not yet finalised.
findings.matters: A declining HRA reserve combined with unresolved cost pressures in core maintenance areas suggests the council is masking structural service costs through reserve drawdown. With a year-end reserve forecast of £5.388m against a budget of £99.521m, the cushion is shrinking while pressures persist.
findings.figures: Reserve declining from £6.446m to £5.388m (£1.058m draw); HRA budget £99.521m
findings.quote: The HRA reserve balance is forecast to reduce from an opening position of £6.446m to £5.388m at year-end, reflecting the planned use of balances to support the revenue position in line with budget expectations.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - NK
findings.headline: Council is financing £4m of approved budget from reserves while waiting for a planned cuts programme to deliver
findings.detail: The agreed 2026-27 budget of £346m includes £4m drawn from the Budget Sustainability Reserve explicitly "to allow time for a planned schedule of cuts and efficiencies." This means the council cannot balance current operations and is deliberately depleting reserves pending future savings.
findings.matters: Reserve financing of operations indicates current revenues cannot cover current spending. If the planned cuts schedule slips or only partially lands, reserve depletion accelerates and leaves the council vulnerable in future years. This is a material structural issue, not a one-off timing gap.
findings.figures: £4.000m Budget Sustainability Reserve draw; net budget £346.005m
findings.quote: The budget included £4.000m of Council financing from the Budget Sustainability Reserve to allow time for a planned schedule of cuts and efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget – First Quarter Review 2026-27 - NK
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £6.9m growing at £3.1m per quarter from uncontrolled high-needs spending
findings.detail: The DSG is projected to overspend by £3.111m in the first quarter alone, creating a cumulative reserve deficit of £6.903m. While government funding covers 90% of high-needs deficits, the council faces material exposure on the remaining 10%. A high-needs review is ongoing but mitigating actions remain to be implemented.
findings.matters: A £6.9m deficit in high-needs education signals structural demand that the council cannot contain. Even with government support, the council's 10% exposure is substantial, and the statutory override protecting the general fund from DSG deficits expires 31 March 2028, at which point deficits could transfer to general fund pressures.
findings.figures: £3.111m Q1 overspend; total deficit £6.903m against budget of £147.289m
findings.quote: The projected outturn at the first quarter on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is an overspend of £3.111m against a budget of £147.289m. This results in a projected deficit on the DSG reserve of £6.903m.

findings.headline: Overall budget delivery is heavily dependent on one-off airport dividend of £6.810m
findings.detail: The council reports a provisional underspend of £8.401m, but this includes a one-off income of £6.810m from the council's shareholding in Newcastle International Airport. Excluding the airport dividend, the operational underspend was only £1.661m. The underlying position masks real demand pressures being held down only by one-off income and use of the Budget Sustainability Reserve (£8.500m used in 2025-26).
findings.matters: One-off income is not sustainable; the council is covering structural overspends (social care, DSG, HRA pressures) with non-recurring revenue and reserve depletion, not operational balance.
findings.figures: One-off airport dividend £6.810m; operational underspend before airport £1.661m; Budget Sustainability Reserve used £8.500m
findings.quote: The significant favourable variance is due to one-off income from the Council's shareholding in Newcastle International Airport.

findings.headline: HRA reserve declining under structural pressure from void loss, disrepair claims, and rising repair costs
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account opening reserve was £10.720m and closed at £6.446m. While the 2025-26 outturn shows a small underspend (£1.142m), the paper explicitly flags that the main budget pressures come from void loss, disrepair claims, and rising repair costs—issues that are not being solved operationally but are being absorbed by reserve depletion.
findings.matters: HRA reserves fund the housing capital programme and service delivery; declining reserves at a time when repair pressures are rising indicates the council is financing repairs from reserves rather than securing sustainable funding.
findings.figures: Opening HRA reserve £10.720m, closing £6.446m; HRA forecasted underspend £1.142m despite noted pressures
findings.quote: The main areas of pressure upon the HRA come from void loss, disrepair claims and rising repair costs.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £1.445m reflects ongoing demand and unresolved health funding gaps
findings.detail: Adult Social Care budgeted £103.078m but spent £104.523m. The paper cites complex high-cost care needs, transition cases, and hospital discharges, plus care packages where health funding is not yet agreed or fully secured. Actions have mitigated some in-year impact but underlying demand remains unaddressed.
findings.matters: A council-wide pattern: social care overspends (adult and children combined £7.385m) suggest structural demand management issues that will persist and likely worsen.
findings.figures: £1.445m overspend on £103.078m budget
findings.quote: The adverse position reflects ongoing demand-led pressures and the impact of complex, high‑cost care needs, including transition cases and hospital discharges. There are also funding pressures relating to care packages where health funding contributions are not yet agreed or fully secured.

findings.headline: DSG deficit accumulating to £3.792m, with statutory override ending 31 March 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (£138.322m budget, £141.508m outturn) shows a £3.176m overspend, primarily from the High Needs Block (SEND support) overspending by £4.842m. The DSG reserve deficit worsened from -£0.616m opening to -£3.792m closing. Currently held separately under statutory override, but the override expires in 2028, at which point this deficit will hit the General Fund.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit represents a time-limited deferral of a real financial problem; lenders need to understand the council's plan to close this gap before the statutory override ends.
findings.figures: DSG overspend £3.176m; High Needs Block overspend £4.842m; DSG reserve deficit £3.792m at 31 March 2026; statutory override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The DSG reserve opening balance was a deficit of £0.616m, which as at 31 March 2026 decreased to a deficit balance of £3.792m, factoring in the 2025/26 overspend. In line with the current statutory override, the deficit balance on the DSG is held separately and is not charged to the Council's General Fund. The statutory override is now due to end on 31 March 2028.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care has a £5.940m structural overspend (10.5% above budget) driven by high-cost external placements
findings.detail: The council budgeted £56.475m for Children's Social Care but spent £62.415m. The paper attributes this to demand pressures from complex-needs placements and limited local provision forcing reliance on expensive external providers. A recovery plan aims to expand local provision and strengthen early intervention, but the underlying demand pressure remains unresolved.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off variance; it reflects structural inability to manage demand within budget, which directly affects future affordability and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £5.940m overspend on £56.475m budget (10.5% overage); recovery plan mentioned but not detailed
findings.quote: sustained demand pressures, particularly from high‑cost placements for children with complex needs. Limited local provision and market pressures have resulted in continued reliance on external placements. A recovery plan is in place to expand local provision and strengthen early intervention with the aim of reducing cost pressures over time.

findings.paper_title: Review of Effectiveness Audit and Standards Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: No formal action plan yet exists to address governance weaknesses identified in this assessment
findings.detail: The self-assessment identifies multiple areas needing improvement (Q15, Q16, Q17, Q28) but states the action plan to remedy these has not yet been drafted. It will be 'drafted and circulated to the members of the Committee for comment' after this assessment is approved.
findings.matters: Identifying governance gaps is valueless without a concrete plan to close them; a lender needs assurance that weaknesses will actually be remediated with timescales and accountability.
findings.figures: Question 28 score: 2 (Moderate Improvement needed); overall score 202/215 but improvement plan not yet drafted
findings.quote: Action Plan to address the necessary improvements identified from this Assessment will be drafted and circulated to the members of the Committee for comment.

findings.paper_title: Review of Effectiveness Audit and Standards Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: Committee members' skills and knowledge have not been formally evaluated since April 2019—over six years ago
findings.detail: The self-assessment identifies that knowledge levels across committee membership are inadequate (score 2). The most recent skills self-assessment dates to April 2019, and though the assessment notes it will be revisited, no updated evaluation has been completed. Training was delivered in 2024/25 but capability assessment remains outstanding.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the audit committee has adequate expertise to scrutinise financial management and controls; an outdated skills assessment leaves uncertainty about whether members can effectively discharge their oversight responsibilities.
findings.figures: Question 15 score: 2 (Moderate Improvement needed); Question 17 score: 2; last skills assessment April 2019
findings.quote: Skills self assessment was circulated in April 2019, will be revisited to inform the revised Development Plan.

findings.paper_title: Review of Effectiveness Audit and Standards Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit committee has been merged with Standards function rather than remaining dedicated oversight
findings.detail: The audit function is combined with Standards responsibilities, which this self-assessment scores as needing significant improvement against CIPFA 2022 guidance. The merger was implemented in 2014. CIPFA recommends a dedicated audit committee to ensure adequate focus on financial oversight.
findings.matters: Audit committee competency and independence directly affect financial oversight quality; combining audit with standards reduces dedicated scrutiny of finance and control arrangements.
findings.figures: Question 1: Significant Improvement needed (score 3 of 5); structure implemented 13 May 2014
findings.quote: Does the authority have a dedicated audit committee that is not combined with other functions (e.g. standards, ethics, scrutiny)? Merged with Standards Committee reported to Cabinet 13 May 2014

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Policy Statement and Treasury Strategy 202627 to 203031 A
findings.headline: Significant concentrations of non-treasury investment in three counterparties with extended maturity
findings.detail: Appendix 8 discloses material holdings in Keelman Homes (£14.55m loan), Newcastle Airport (£17.09m shareholding plus £12.9m loan notes), and Citizens Advice Bureau (£370k loan). The airport loan notes have principal repayment deferred until 2032. These are non-liquid, counterparty-specific risks not managed as normal treasury.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of material off-treasury investments and any impairment risk. The concentration in airport and housing company investment exposes the Council to sector-specific shocks.
findings.figures: Newcastle Airport total exposure: £30.0m (shareholding £17.1m + loan notes £12.9m); Keelman Homes: £14.55m; total identifiable non-treasury investments: £53.87m
findings.quote: Non-Treasury Management Investments: Long term loans to Keelman Homes £14,553,560; Newcastle International Airport £17,091,970 (13.33% shareholding); Newcastle International Airport Long Term credit notes £12,900,414 (Principal repayment due 2032)

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Policy Statement and Treasury Strategy 202627 to 203031 A
findings.headline: Council pursuing internal borrowing strategy, drawing on reserves rather than external markets
findings.detail: The Council is deliberately using internal borrowing (drawing down reserves) as a short-term funding strategy because investment returns (forecast 3.25% by 2027) are lower than external borrowing costs. This is described as cost-saving but creates a 'cost of carry' risk if rates move unexpectedly.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether reserves are being systematically depleted, whether the Council can reverse this if rates spike, and whether the strategy leaves adequate liquidity reserves.
findings.figures: Net debt (excluding PFI) as of 31 January 2026: £608.387m (borrowing £655.182m less investments £46.795m)
findings.quote: External borrowing rates currently exceed the return available for investments, meaning savings can be achieved by borrowing internally from reserves in the short term. The current policy of internal borrowing will continue to be followed as a short-term funding option serving to minimise overall cost.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Policy Statement and Treasury Strategy 202627 to 203031 A
findings.headline: Authorized borrowing to grow from £844m to £1,026m over five years
findings.detail: The Council's authorized limit for external debt—the maximum it can borrow—is set to increase by £182m (21.6%) between 2026/27 and 2030/31. The Operational Boundary also rises from £829m to £1,011m. This reflects increasing capital programmes over the period.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the Council can service significantly higher debt levels, particularly if economic forecasts change or capital receipts fall short.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit 2026/27: £844m; Authorised Limit 2030/31: £1,026m; increase of £182m
findings.quote: It is a statutory requirement of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, for the Council to produce a balanced budget. In particular, Section 31(a), as amended by the Localism Act 2011, requires a local authority to calculate its budget requirement for each financial year to include the revenue costs that flow from capital financing decisions.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Policy Statement and Treasury Strategy 202627 to 203031 A
findings.headline: Council increasing concentration risk per counterparty from 20% to 25% of total investments
findings.detail: Following a review, the Council has raised the maximum limit of investments per counterparty from 20% to 25% of total investment holdings or £20m, whichever is lower. This concentrates exposure to individual institutions during a period when the Council holds £46.795m in total investments.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the Council's portfolio concentration creates a liquidity or credit event risk if a major counterparty experiences problems.
findings.figures: Total investments as of 31 January 2026: £46.795m; previous limit: 20%; new limit: 25%
findings.quote: Following a review of investment balances the % limit per counterparty has been revised to not exceed a maximum limit equal to 25% (previously 20%) of total investments or £20m.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Treasury Policy Statement and Treasury Strategy 202627 to 203031 A
findings.headline: Commercial investment income forecast to drop by a quarter in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council's income from financial investments is falling from £4.577m in 2025/26 to £3.434m from 2026/27 onwards. This represents a 25% reduction in non-service revenue from treasury and commercial investments. The decline is driven by lower forecast interest rates and is expected to persist through the five-year strategy period.
findings.matters: A lender would care whether the Council can sustain its forecast position if income falls further than projected, particularly given the growing authorized borrowing levels and the internal borrowing strategy.
findings.figures: Income from financial investments: £4,577k (2025/26) vs £3,434k (2026/27-2030/31); a £1,143k annual reduction
findings.quote: Investment returns are likely to decrease during 2026/27 with further decreases forecast in the following two years.

findings.headline: Redundancy consultation underway with significant pension and severance costs to be met from reserves
findings.detail: A 30-day collective consultation on workforce redundancies commenced on 14 January 2026. The council acknowledges "the cost of the redundancies will require a significant one-off cost in terms of redundancy payments and pension costs which will need to be met from revenue or reserves." The council's scheme is "modestly enhanced," suggesting payments above statutory minimum.
findings.matters: Redundancy costs must be funded from reserves or current revenue, directly consuming the already-thin cash buffer. Large-scale redundancies also reduce council operational capacity, potentially impairing service delivery and future income generation (business support, planning fees). Scale of redundancies signals depth of service cuts required.
findings.figures: Consultation commenced: 14 January 2026; cost described as "significant one-off cost" to be met from revenue or reserves; scheme is "modestly enhanced"
findings.quote: A number of savings proposals have workforce implications which have resulted in roles being placed at risk of redundancy. A 30-day collective consultation period commenced on 14 January 2026 to consider how redundancies might be avoided, reduced or mitigated

findings.headline: £4.5m collection fund deficit from 2025/26 reduces available cash and signals income weakness
findings.detail: The council must absorb a £4.497m shortfall on its Collection Fund from 2025/26, comprising £1.654m from Council Tax under-performance and £2.843m from business rates. This deficit reduces cash available for 2026/27 services and signals either resident inability to pay Council Tax or economic weakness affecting business rates collection.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits indicate underlying economic stress. If residents cannot pay Council Tax due to cost-of-living pressures, or if business rates fall due to economic contraction, both signal future income vulnerability. The £4.5m cannot be used for services, forcing additional cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Collection Fund deficit 2025/26: £4.497m (Council Tax £1.654m, NNDR £2.843m); represents 1.3% of 2026/27 net budget
findings.quote: The proposed budget includes an estimated deficit of £4.497m, which comprises of a deficit on Council Tax of £1.654m and a deficit on National Non-Domestic Rates (NNDR) of £2.843m.

findings.headline: Growing number of schools facing deficits as funding growth of 2.4% cannot cover pay and utility cost rises
findings.detail: The Department for Education is providing only 2.4% per-pupil funding growth to mainstream schools, with a 0% minimum funding guarantee. Schools must absorb higher pay awards and rising utilities that significantly exceed this rate. The council explicitly states that "the number of schools with projected deficits is increasing" and that "some schools will continue to be under financial pressure due to falling rolls."
findings.matters: Growing school deficits create a contingent liability. Schools with persistent deficits may eventually require council intervention or closure, forcing additional expenditure on an already-stretched budget. School financial deterioration also signals potential reductions in educational quality, which creates future social and economic costs.
findings.figures: DfE funding growth: 2.4% per-pupil increase; minimum funding guarantee: 0% after grants; council notes school deficit numbers are increasing
findings.quote: The number of schools with projected deficits is increasing. The DfE has estimated 2.4% increased funding to mainstream on a per pupil basis, however this funding will not cover the full cost of the estimated 2026/27 pay rises and the increased cost of utilities and services

findings.headline: Adult social care demand will rise 50% among oldest residents by 2045, driven by aging and labor cost inflation
findings.detail: The 80+ population (those with greatest care needs) will grow from 11,300 to 17,000 by 2045—a 50% increase. The 2026/27 budget already includes £5.535m for adult social care pressures, mainly from rising external provider fees. The council explicitly notes that National Living Wage increases mean service providers are recovering costs through annual inflationary uplifts to contract prices.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a statutory responsibility the council cannot avoid or cut. Demographic growth in demand is structural and unavoidable, and compounds with labor cost inflation. This creates a long-term cost pressure that will persist regardless of council priorities, crowding out other services and constraining future flexibility.
findings.figures: Population aged 80+: 11,300 (2025) to 17,000 (2045), a 50% increase; £5.535m for adult social care demand pressures in 2026/27
findings.quote: the number of people aged 80 years and over (i.e. those generally with the greatest care needs) is forecast to rise from around 11,300 in 2025 to 17,000 in 2045 (an increase of 50%)

findings.headline: Council faces £42.054m funding gap over five years with no detailed solution yet agreed
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy projects a £42.054m shortfall from 2026/27 to 2030/31. The council states this will be met through budget cuts and social care interventions, but specific plans remain under development. The council notes work is "ongoing to refresh the MTFS" and that "the Council will identify savings opportunities" through its annual planning cycle.
findings.matters: A £42m gap over five years represents 12% of the current budget. The absence of detailed, agreed solutions creates uncertainty about service viability. If assumed savings do not materialize—from demand management or income growth—the council will face forced choices between underfunded services, emergency borrowing, or further tax increases.
findings.figures: Five-year MTFS gap: £42.054m (2026/27 to 2030/31); current net budget: £346.005m
findings.quote: The MTFS has estimated a gap of £42.054m over five years which is to be met through budget cuts and social care interventions.

findings.headline: Budget Sustainability Reserve will be completely exhausted by March 2027
findings.detail: The council's Budget Sustainability reserve stood at £17.2m in April 2025 but will fall to zero by March 2027. In 2026/27 alone, £4m will be drawn to balance the budget. Once this reserve is gone, the council will have no specialized buffer for financial shocks beyond its General Fund Balance, forcing future pressures to be met through deeper cuts, borrowing, or tax increases.
findings.matters: Reserve exhaustion signals the council has spent down its financial buffers. When dedicated reserves are depleted, the council loses flexibility to absorb unexpected costs or timing misalignments. This increases risk of mid-year emergency borrowing or forced service cuts.
findings.figures: Budget Sustainability reserve: £17.175m (1 April 2025) declining to £0.000m (31 March 2027); £4.000m withdrawn in 2026/27
findings.quote: The proposed 2026/27 base budget includes £4.000m use of the Budget Sustainability reserve, and £0.921m budgeted use of strategic earmarked reserves (Financial Risk and Resilience £0.155m and Thrive £0.766m) in support of Council priorities

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: HRA viability structurally dependent on applying maximum permitted 4.8% rent increase; 1% shortfall costs £0.8m annually
findings.detail: The council notes that applying less than the maximum 4.8% rent increase would have 'a significant impact on viability of the HRA' because any reduction would permanently lower the rent base for all future years. A 1% reduction would cost approximately £0.8m in 2026/27 rent revenue alone, suggesting narrow operating margins.
findings.matters: Structural dependence on maximum permitted rent increases indicates tight underlying cash flow with limited margin for affordability concessions or policy flexibility.
findings.figures: 4.8% maximum permitted increase; £0.8m annual revenue impact of 1% reduction
findings.quote: Not applying the maximum rent increase of 4.8% is an option but this would have a significant impact on viability of the HRA as any increase below this level would reduce the base rent figure upon which all future rent increases would be calculated. For example, a 1% change would reduce an indicative rent revenue in 2026/27 alone by an estimated £0.8m.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: 30-year HRA Business Plan requires borrowing to rise significantly above current levels to fund capital investment programme
findings.detail: Although the approved 30-year HRA Business Plan maintains minimum reserves throughout, the document explicitly states that 'borrowing will need to rise significantly above the current levels' to fund anticipated capital investment including new social housing stock and existing stock maintenance.
findings.matters: Materially higher HRA debt service costs will increase future rent pressure and reduce the council's financial flexibility. Projections of 'significant' borrowing growth indicate structural capital demand.
findings.figures: No specific borrowing quantum provided; characterised as 'significantly above the current levels'
findings.quote: However, over the long term, to incorporate all the cost pressures and anticipated capital investment, including new social housing stock, borrowing will need to rise significantly above the current levels.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: HRA reserve headroom above minimum floor tightening from £2.204m to £1.146m in a single year
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires £1.058m drawdown from reserves. Projected closing balance falls to £4.146m against a 30-year minimum requirement of £3m, leaving only £1.146m headroom above the floor. This represents a 48% reduction in financial buffer capacity year-on-year.
findings.matters: Narrowing reserve headroom reduces the HRA's shock absorption capacity against unexpected costs, income shortfalls, or welfare reform impacts. Limited headroom constrains future policy flexibility.
findings.figures: Opening balance 2026/27: £5.204m; closing balance: £4.146m; minimum requirement: £3m; headroom: £1.146m
findings.quote: The proposed HRA budget 2026/27 will require the use of £1.058m of HRA Reserves. As at 31 March 2027 the HRA reserve is projected to be £4.146m. The 30-year HRA Business plan is sustainable with a minimum balance of £3m of reserves maintained per annum.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: Damp and mould repair complexity emerging as cost pressure driving 2025/26 overspend
findings.detail: The HRA is currently projecting a £0.099m overspend for 2025/26, with the document citing 'a significant increase in the complexity of repairs, particularly damp and mould related repair requests' alongside 'high contractor costs' as drivers. This emerging pressure is not yet reflected as a line in 2026/27 budget adjustments.
findings.matters: If damp and mould repair costs continue to exceed budget, the HRA will need additional reserve drawdown or spending cuts, eroding financial headroom and reducing capital investment capacity.
findings.figures: 2025/26 overspend: £0.099m; 2026/27 repairs budget: £34.218m (down from 2025/26 budget of £35.991m)
findings.quote: The HRA projected outturn 2025/26 at the third quarter is an overspend of £0.099m and this is incorporated into the HRA budget to reflect the estimated reserve balance at 31 March 2026. The overspend is being driven by several factors: continued inflationary pressures, a significant increase in the complexity of repairs, particularly damp and mould related repair requests, high contractor costs, void rent loss and council tax, an ageing housing stock, additional unfunded new burdens, the need for HRA reform.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: Uneconomic housing stock identified where required investment significantly exceeds rental income; appraisal pending
findings.detail: The council has identified housing schemes where 'the required expenditure on some schemes over the short and longer term significantly exceeds any income from those schemes due to poor or no demand, coupled with the need for high value investment works'. An appraisal of available options is outstanding, suggesting potential disposal or write-down.
findings.matters: Uneconomic assets may require subsidy from operating revenue or asset write-offs, reducing capital available for reinvestment and creating an ongoing drain on HRA finances.
findings.figures: Quantum of uneconomic stock not quantified in this budget
findings.quote: Address uneconomic and poor performing housing stock in Gateshead. Stock condition and demand information confirms that the required expenditure on some schemes over the short and longer term significantly exceeds any income from those schemes due to poor or no demand, coupled with the need for high value investment works. There is an outstanding need to appraise all available options for these schemes over the coming months.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Housing Capital Programme
findings.headline: Universal Credit recipients now 58.1% of tenants with rent collection 2.06 percentage points lower than other tenants
findings.detail: As of February 2026, 9,958 council tenants (58.1% of the 17,772-unit social rent stock) receive Universal Credit, a share that 'will continue to increase'. Rent collection from UC claimants is 97.94% compared to around 100% for other tenants. This represents a structural decline in collection efficacy as the UC-dependent tenant base grows.
findings.matters: Lower collection rates reduce HRA cash flow for maintenance and debt service. A permanent shift in the tenant base to lower-collecting UC recipients creates an ongoing drag on operating income.
findings.figures: 9,958 UC claimants = 58.1% of stock; 97.94% vs ~100% collection rate differential
findings.quote: As at 3 February 2026, 9,958 (58.1%) of council tenants were in receipt of UC payments, and this will continue to increase as new claims or change of circumstances are submitted. Rent collection rates for UC claimants is 97.94% compared to around 100% for other tenants.

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates at 5.46% significantly higher than budget assumptions, increasing future debt servicing costs
findings.detail: PWLB rates at the end of December 2025 stand at 5.46%, higher than the original budget assumptions. Any borrowing taken at these rates will create higher revenue costs for debt servicing than was originally planned.
findings.matters: Higher than expected borrowing costs will require either revenue reallocation or capital programme adjustment. This affects financial flexibility and medium-term budget planning.
findings.figures: 5.46% PWLB rates at end December 2025; current average interest rate on existing borrowing 3.56%
findings.quote: PWLB borrowing costs have fluctuated in year, with borrowing rates at end of December 2025 at 5.46%. PWLB rates are currently higher than budgeted and will be monitored to ensure any borrowing is taken at the optimum time to minimise the number of long term loans entered into at the current higher level of interest rates.

findings.headline: Liability benchmark shows under-borrowed position requiring external borrowing before year end
findings.detail: The council's liability benchmark calculation indicates that external debt is below the benchmark level, meaning the council will need to take some external borrowing in 2025/26 despite efforts to delay. This borrowing will likely occur at the current higher rate of 5.46%.
findings.matters: The council cannot avoid borrowing indefinitely; they will eventually have to borrow at high rates, creating revenue cost pressure. This reduces the benefit of the delay strategy.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed position identified in Appendix 3 liability benchmark as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: The Liability Benchmark gross loans requirement, subject to using internal borrowing and maintaining a liquidity allowance in Treasury Management investments, indicates external debt is below the benchmark and shows that we are in an under-borrowed position in 2025/26, indicating that we will need to take some external borrowing this year.

findings.headline: No borrowing taken in 2025/26 despite planned £88.4m requirement, waiting for rates to fall
findings.detail: The council originally planned to borrow £88.438m in 2025/26 but has taken no new borrowing. PWLB rates at end December 2025 stand at 5.46%, which is higher than budgeted. The council is monitoring rates and timing borrowing to minimise costs.
findings.matters: This creates timing and rate risk; eventually the council will need to borrow at potentially sustained high rates. Delaying locks in higher future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £88.438m original borrowing requirement vs £0m taken to date; 5.46% PWLB rates at end December
findings.quote: Due to the current high long-term borrowing rates there has been no borrowing taken in the year to date.

findings.headline: Investment income projected £1.8m below budget due to lower cash balances from borrowing delay
findings.detail: Budgeted investment income was £3.926m but is now projected at only £2.121m. The council deliberately delayed borrowing to avoid high interest rates, keeping cash balances lower than expected and earning less on investments. Combined with falling interest rates, this reduces net interest to the General Fund from £5.455m budget to £4.130m.
findings.matters: Lower investment returns represent a £1.3m hit to the revenue budget; the council is banking on eventually borrowing at lower rates to recover this cost.
findings.figures: £3.926m budgeted vs £2.121m projected investment income; £5.455m budgeted vs £4.130m projected net interest; £1.325m variance
findings.quote: The £1.325m variance to budget is due to the strategy of delaying borrowing meaning investment balances are lower than estimated.

findings.headline: Management interventions during 2025/26 are assumed necessary to deliver the HRA to budget
findings.detail: The cover report states that it is 'assumed' management interventions during 2025/26 will enable the HRA to be delivered on budget. This indicates the plan is contingent on specific management actions in the current year, suggesting baseline pressures without these interventions.
findings.matters: Reliance on unspecified management interventions to achieve budget is a near-term financial risk; failure to deliver these actions could result in overspend or reserve drawdown in 2025/26
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: it is assumed that management interventions during 2025/26 will enable the HRA to be delivered on budget

findings.headline: Medium-term efficiency savings are required as part of the plan to support capital investment
findings.detail: The business plan identifies that efficiency savings will be needed alongside increased borrowing to support the financial trajectory and capital investment programme. The scale and timing of these savings is not detailed in this cover report.
findings.matters: Required savings are a leading indicator of budget risk; if these savings do not materialise, reserve drawdown or service reductions will follow, affecting housing delivery and financial stability
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: over the longer term borrowing will need rise significantly above the current levels and medium-term efficiency savings will be required

findings.headline: Borrowing will need to rise significantly above current levels to fund capital investment including new social housing
findings.detail: The plan incorporates substantial capital investment for housing stock and new build schemes. To fund this investment over the 30-year period, HRA borrowing is projected to increase significantly beyond current levels. This is presented as a necessary consequence of the planned capital programme.
findings.matters: Rising HRA borrowing is a material strategic financial commitment that affects the council's total debt position, its overall creditworthiness, and the sustainability of housing services
findings.figures: No specific borrowing figures provided; stated only as 'significantly above the current levels'
findings.quote: over the longer term borrowing will need rise significantly above the current levels and medium-term efficiency savings will be required

findings.headline: Debtor balances misclassified within financial statement notes; errors are individually trivial but aggregate to £3.517m when extrapolated
findings.detail: Testing identified two debtor balances that were classified incorrectly within the notes to the accounts and should have appeared in different disclosure lines. While each misclassification is trivial in isolation, they exceed the trivial threshold in aggregate and extrapolate to a non-trivial, non-material balance of £3.517m, indicating systematic classification issues in debtor processing.
findings.matters: Systematic errors in debtor classification suggest weaknesses in the council's financial reporting controls that could mask larger issues and indicate that receivable balances cannot be reliably identified and tracked.
findings.figures: £3.517m extrapolated error from sample testing
findings.quote: Our testing of debtors identified two debtor balances disclosed within the Other Entities and Individuals line in note 22 that had been misclassified and should have been included in other lines within the Note. These misclassifications are trivial when considered individually, but above trivial in aggregate and extrapolate to a non-trivial, non-material balance of £3.517m.

findings.headline: Surplus asset revalued downward by £1.4m following discovery it had been omitted from annual revaluation cycle
findings.detail: During audit testing, one land asset classified as a surplus asset was found to have not been revalued in the year. Once revalued by the council's valuer, the asset's value decreased from £5.9m to £4.5m, representing a £1.4m reduction. This material misstatement has been adjusted in the accounts.
findings.matters: A reduction in the council's capital asset base indicates either that property values are falling or the asset was previously overvalued, both of which are material to lenders assessing the council's financial stability and collateral position.
findings.figures: £1.4m decrease; asset revalued from £5.9m to £4.5m
findings.quote: The Council subsequently requested a valuation from their valuer, which resulted in a decreased in the land value from £5.9m to £4.5m. The movement of £1.4m has been reported as an adjusted error – see page 24 of this report.

findings.headline: Gateshead Energy Company consolidated into group accounts for the first time due to material increase in property holdings
findings.detail: In the prior year (2023/24), the Council determined that group accounts were not required as the subsidiary had no material balances. However, during 2024/25, the property, plant and equipment balance within Gateshead Energy Company increased materially, prompting the Council to prepare consolidated group accounts for 2024/25 for the first time, consolidating the subsidiary's position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's full consolidated financial position including all subsidiaries. A material change in a subsidiary's capital base could indicate new investments, operational changes, or emerging financial risks that affect the council's overall creditworthiness.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided for the increase
findings.quote: The Council confirmed that during 2024/25 the PPE balance held within the Gateshead Energy Company had increased and as such the Council deemed it necessary to prepare group accounts for 2024/25 which consolidates the Council's subsidiary, Gateshead Energy Company.

findings.headline: Material discrepancy remains unresolved between actual pensionable pay and actuary's estimate affecting pension liability valuation
findings.detail: The audit has identified an outstanding material difference between the Council's actual pensionable pay and the estimated pensionable pay figure used by the actuary in their IAS19 pension calculations. As of the audit completion report date, this remains unresolved and is being discussed with the Pension Fund auditor. The pension position comprises gross assets of £1,621.96m and gross liabilities of £1,311.06m.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities typically represent one of the largest balance sheet items for councils. A material discrepancy in the inputs used to calculate the liability could mean the reported pension asset/liability position is significantly misstated, affecting the council's overall financial position.
findings.figures: Gross pension assets £1,621.96m, gross pension liabilities £1,311.06m
findings.quote: We note that we have outstanding queries in relation to a material difference identified between the actual pensionable pay of the Council and the estimated pensionable pay used by the Actuary in their IAS19 report calculations.

findings.headline: Cash reconciliation timing difference of £0.730m at year-end, affecting debtor balances
findings.detail: A recurring timing difference of £0.730m was identified between the council's cash records and bank statements at 31 March 2025. This caused cash to be understated and debtors overstated by £0.665m on the balance sheet, though it reverses in April. Management proposes to adjust in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Recurring year-end timing issues in cash and debtors suggest control gaps in period-end reconciliation and cash management processes
findings.figures: £0.730m timing difference; £0.665m balance sheet impact
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025, a recurring timing difference of £0.730m was identified between the Exchequer Services cashbook and the Council's bank account, primarily due to end-of day cut-off procedures. This resulted in an understatement of cash and overstatement of debtors by £0.665m on the balance sheet.

findings.headline: Debtor classification errors extrapolate to £3.517m across the council's receivables
findings.detail: Auditor testing found misclassifications of debtor balances in Note 22. While individual errors were trivial, the sample testing extrapolates to a total error of £3.517m when applied to all debtors. Management did not correct these errors.
findings.matters: Systematic misclassification of receivables indicates control weaknesses in how the council tracks and categorises money owed to it, affecting debtor reporting reliability
findings.figures: £3.517m extrapolated
findings.quote: These misclassifications are trivial when considered individually, but above trivial in aggregate and extrapolate to a non-trivial, non-material balance of £3.517m.

findings.headline: Heritage assets valuation unsupported by audit evidence, creating £5.564m unadjusted misstatement
findings.detail: The council's valuation of certain heritage assets lacked sufficient audit evidence. This resulted in a £5.564m misstatement that auditors identified but management chose not to correct. The existence of evidence gaps in asset valuation suggests control weaknesses in the asset valuation process.
findings.matters: Weak evidence supporting major asset valuations raises questions about the reliability of the balance sheet and the council's controls over valuation processes
findings.quote: The misstatement arose due to the Council not having sufficient evidence to support the valuation of certain heritage assets

findings.headline: Overall financial sustainability is rated Red 35 unmitigated due to government funding cuts, lost income, and demand pressures outpacing controls.
findings.detail: RD-S01 (Financial Sustainability of the Council) is Red 35 unmitigated—one of the highest-rated risks in the register—and only mitigated to Amber 12. The risk explicitly notes impact on 'reserve levels, quantum of cuts and ability to plan cuts,' as well as rogue spend or Major Project overspends due to inadequate controls.
findings.matters: This is the council's core financial viability risk; a lender needs to understand whether reserves are being drawn to cover structural deficits and whether the council can plan capital spending given the need for cuts.
findings.figures: RD-S01: Red 35 unmitigated, Amber 12 mitigated. Impacts 'reserve levels, quantum of cuts and ability to plan cuts.'
findings.quote: Inadequate internal controls and governance could lead to rogue spend or an increased risk of a significant overspend or underspend being reported on Capital / Major Projects. This could impact on reserve levels, quantum of cuts and ability to plan cuts.

findings.headline: School place demand is shifting, creating unfunded secondary provision obligations while reducing primary school budgets.
findings.detail: CSCLL-S02 shows 16% fewer primary school places needed in 3–5 years, but increasing secondary demand. Primary schools will operate below the 30-pupil optimum, impacting their budgets; the Council must finance additional secondary places, creating a net cost pressure despite reduced primary demand.
findings.matters: Capital investment in secondary provision is an unfunded obligation during a period of demand-led service pressures; it further constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 16% fewer primary places needed over 3–5 years; offsetting increase in secondary demand requiring Council-financed additional places
findings.quote: The decrease in demand for primary school places is not enough to require the closure of schools, but will impact on primary school budgets as class numbers will fall below the optimum of 30 children (or 15 for a split class). The Council will need to finance additional secondary school places which also has a financial / budgetary impact for the Council.

findings.headline: Adult social care funding faces specific, uncontrollable cost pressures from National Insurance and National Living Wage increases.
findings.detail: IASCS-S03 flags that 'the Council has limited or no opportunity to influence National government decisions regarding changes in policy or taxation which will affect the Council financially (for example, National Insurance and National Living Wage increases).' Red 35 unmitigated, mitigated only to Amber 9 due to forecasting challenges and limited control.
findings.matters: These are legislated cost increases the council must absorb with limited flexibility; they reduce the council's financial headroom and increase the need for savings or borrowing elsewhere.
findings.figures: IASCS-S03: Red 35 unmitigated, Amber 9 mitigated
findings.quote: In some cases, the Council has limited or no opportunity to influence National government decisions regarding changes in policy or taxation which will affect the Council financially (for example, National Insurance and National Living Wage increases).

findings.headline: Treasury management and borrowing strategy carries extreme unmitigated risk of interest rate loss or sub-optimal financing.
findings.detail: RD-S04 is rated Red 21 unmitigated (Extreme/Catastrophic impact 7, Moderate likelihood 3), addressing 'failure to implement a sound Treasury Management Investment and Borrowing Strategy, resulting in loss of resources or a less than optimum interest rate position.' Mitigation brings it to Amber 7, but the unmitigated risk is severe.
findings.matters: Sub-optimal treasury decisions directly impact the council's ability to service debt and maintain financial stability; this risk explicitly concerns loss of resources.
findings.figures: RD-S04: Red 21 unmitigated, Amber 7 mitigated
findings.quote: This risk if realised could impact directly on the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Children's and adults' social care demand continues to outpace capacity despite mitigation efforts, with Red-rated risks remaining after controls.
findings.detail: Four social care risks remain rated Red or high after mitigation (CSCLL-S03 Red 21, CSCLL-S05 Red 21, IASCS-S01 Red 21, IASCS-S02 Red 21). Children are being placed in out-of-borough high-cost and unregulated arrangements; adults' social care faces demand it cannot minimise. Staffing shortages in social care are described as Almost Certain (likelihood 5), and immigration policy changes may create a 'cliff edge' the Council cannot control.
findings.matters: Unfunded demand growth in social care—especially when combined with government cost pressures councils can't control—directly pressures reserves and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: CSCLL-S03 and IASCS-S01 both Red 35 unmitigated, Red 21 after controls. CSCLL-S05 and IASCS-S02 Red 35 unmitigated, Red 21 after controls.
findings.quote: Providing additional years of SEND support has a significant financial impact on the Council, which could reduce available budget for the delivery of other vital services.

findings.paper_title: Report_Audit Completion and Statement of Accounts
findings.headline: Audit opinion conditional on resolving outstanding pension matters
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars anticipate issuing an unqualified opinion on the financial statements, but explicitly note this is subject to satisfactory conclusion of remaining work on pension matters. The audit work relies on Ernst and Young's assurance on Tyne and Wear Pension Fund disclosures, and this work remains incomplete.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically a material element of council balance sheets; unresolved audit matters in this area represent a risk to financial statement sign-off and could indicate issues with liability measurement or disclosure.
findings.figures: Not specified in this summary document
findings.quote: At the time of issuing the report, and subject to satisfactory conclusion of the remaining audit work, Forvis Mazars anticipate issuing an unqualified opinion, without modification, on the financial statements. However, this is subject to the conclusion of matters in relation to pensions.

findings.headline: Interest payable forecasts are £1.606m below budget due to PWLB rates being lower than expected, generating an offsetting saving to the investment income shortfall.
findings.detail: Forecast interest payable is £24.529m (General Fund £12.655m + HRA £11.874m) against a budget of £26.135m, delivering a gross saving of £1.606m. This saving substantially offsets the £1.519m shortfall in investment income, resulting in a small net underspend of £0.087m overall.
findings.matters: The treasury position remains broadly neutral year-to-date despite the investment income miss, because lower borrowing costs offset it. This shows the council's treasury management is managing the combined risk of investment and borrowing positions.
findings.figures: Forecast £24.529m vs budget £26.135m; saving £1.606m
findings.quote: This represents a gross saving of £1.606m on the original estimate.

findings.headline: Despite planning to borrow £88.438m in 2025/26, the council has taken no new borrowing year-to-date and maintains excess borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: The Treasury Strategy estimated a borrowing need of £88.438m (£58.996m General Fund, £29.442m HRA) but the council has not drawn any new borrowing. This reflects both lower capital financing requirement and deliberate timing around interest rate expectations. The council's total debt stands at £660.182m against an operational limit of £836m.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council is managing debt timing strategically and currently has significant undrawn borrowing capacity, which is a flexibility signal.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £660.182m; Operational limit £836m; Planned borrowing £88.438m, actual new borrowing £0
findings.quote: Due to the council maintaining its cash reserves and a reduction in the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) there has been no borrowing taken in the year to date.

findings.headline: Investment income is £1.519m below budget due to deliberately lower cash balances while waiting for interest rates to fall.
findings.detail: The council projected £3.926m in investment income for 2025/26 but is now forecasting only £2.273m. The council's treasury strategy explicitly delays borrowing until interest rates reduce, meaning investment balances are lower than estimated. This is a strategic choice, not a performance failure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's cash position is being managed tactically around interest rate expectations, and that projected treasury income is now materially lower than budgeted.
findings.figures: £2.273m projected outturn vs £3.926m budget; £1.519m variance
findings.quote: This is mainly due to the treasury management strategy of delaying borrowing until interest rates reduce which means that investment balances are lower than estimated.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand emerging as new cost pressure in 2025/26
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is newly listed among cost pressures for 2025/26. This is an emerging pressure that typically accelerates rapidly and consumes significant resources once it emerges.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs can escalate sharply and are difficult to control; emergence signals worsening housing insecurity and forecast accuracy problems
findings.figures: No amount specified
findings.quote: Increased demand for temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: No balanced budget for 2026/27; council plans to draw reserves through that year with significant funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council has not identified a balanced budget path for 2026/27. The Medium-Term Financial Strategy contains significant uncertainty and will be revisited after the Chancellor's Autumn Statement. The council explicitly states it will be difficult to deliver substantial savings without significant service changes.
findings.matters: A two-year reserve dependency with no identified savings plan represents deteriorating financial sustainability and rising borrowing risk
findings.figures: Reserves to be drawn through 2026/27; no specific savings target identified
findings.quote: The Council acknowledges that it will be difficult to continue to deliver substantial savings without significant changes in the way we deliver services and Cabinet agreed to the planned use of reserves until 2026/27 to smooth and assist transition and mitigate future risk.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care demand remains unresolved with no funded interventions identified
findings.detail: Continued demand for adult and children's social care is listed as a primary cost pressure in 2025/26. The budget strategy references planned demand interventions but provides no specific interventions or funding to address these pressures.
findings.matters: Social care typically consumes 30-40% of council spending; unmet demand without funded solutions represents the largest unfunded pressure on medium-term affordability and future borrowing
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Strong financial management remains critical and the following are the cost pressures currently being faced in 2025/26: Continued demand for Adult Social care services. Continued demand for Children's Social Care services.

findings.headline: 2025/26 budget of £328.768m balanced only through £8.5m reserve draw; Q1 already projecting £1.6m overspend
findings.detail: The council requires £8.5m from the Budget Sustainability Reserve to balance a £328.768m budget. By Q1 (July 2025), despite management interventions, the council was already forecasting a £1.6m revenue overspend. This indicates the budget is unaffordable even with reserve support.
findings.matters: Reserve-dependent budgets are unsustainable; early overspend forecasts signal structural affordability problems and accelerating reserve depletion
findings.figures: £8.5m reserve draw required; £1.6m Q1 projected overspend
findings.quote: The position includes £8.500m of Council financing from the Budget Sustainability Reserve to allow time for a planned schedule of demand interventions and efficiencies. At that time the projected revenue outturn, following management interventions, was an overall projected overspend of £1.6m.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account budgeted for £0.316m surplus but delivered £0.738m overspend in 2024/25
findings.detail: The HRA deteriorated sharply through the year, moving from a planned £0.316m surplus to a £0.738m overspend by Q3. The council drew £0.5m from reserves to cover the deficit. This signals rising housing maintenance or service costs that could spread to general fund pressures.
findings.matters: HRA deficits indicate rising housing maintenance or delivery costs that could escalate further and consume general fund capacity
findings.figures: £0.316m budgeted surplus vs £0.738m actual overspend; £0.5m reserve used to cover
findings.quote: The HRA budget was initially set on 22 February 2024 to deliver a surplus budget of £0.316m however at the third quarter, on 21 January 2025, the projected overspend on the HRA was £0.738m.

findings.headline: School places demand shifting from primary to secondary will impose structural budget costs.
findings.detail: 16% fewer primary school places needed over 3–5 years will reduce primary school budgets as class sizes fall below optimum (30 per class); simultaneously, rising secondary demand will force the council to finance additional secondary places. This creates a structural mismatch the council must finance.
findings.matters: This is unfunded structural change in a major budget area; the council cannot avoid the cost.
findings.figures: CSCLL-S02 unmitigated rating 16 (Likely 4 × High 4); mitigated to Amber 12
findings.quote: The decrease in demand for primary school places is not enough to require the closure of schools, but will impact on primary school budgets as class numbers will fall below the optimum of 30 children (or 15 for a split class). The Council will need to finance additional secondary school places which also has a financial / budgetary impact for the Council.

findings.headline: SEND demand growth will have significant financial impact, competing with other council services.
findings.detail: The council expects children requiring SEND support to be identified much earlier and demand is rising materially. This creates a Red 28 (unmitigated) risk that diverts funding from other services.
findings.matters: Statutory SEND support is unfunded and any rise in identified need directly competes with discretionary services and reserves.
findings.figures: CSCLL-S01 unmitigated rating 28 (Likely 4 × Extreme/Catastrophic 7); mitigated to Amber 12
findings.quote: Providing additional years of SEND support has a significant financial impact on the Council, which could reduce available budget for the delivery of other vital services.

findings.headline: Treasury and borrowing strategy risk could lock in sub-optimal interest rates or lose resources.
findings.detail: Although rated Remote likelihood, the impact is Extreme/Catastrophic. The council has identified a risk of failure to implement sound Treasury Management and Borrowing Strategy that could directly damage financial sustainability through poor interest rate positioning or resource loss.
findings.matters: For a council likely to borrow to cover unfunded demand, a strategic treasury failure is existential; even low probability of this outcome is material to lenders.
findings.figures: RD-S04 unmitigated rating 21 (Moderate 3 × Extreme/Catastrophic 7); mitigated to Amber 7 (Remote 1 × Extreme/Catastrophic 7)
findings.quote: There is a risk of failure to implement a sound Treasury Management Investment and Borrowing Strategy, resulting in loss of resources or a less than optimum interest rate position. This risk if realised could impact directly on the Council's financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account sustainability threatened by loss of central funding and rent income.
findings.detail: The HRA faces almost certain pressure from government funding withdrawal and falling rent income, combined with rising demand and costs. This impacts the council's ability to meet landlord duties and meet savings targets.
findings.matters: The HRA is ringfenced but borrowing against it or cross-subsidy with general fund affects overall council financial resilience.
findings.figures: RD-S02 unmitigated rating 20 (Almost Certain 5 × High 4); mitigated to Amber 9
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Council fails to minimise future financial risks to the ringfenced HRA account (decrease or removal of Central Government Funding and decrease or lost rent income, as well as increasing demand and cost pressures).

findings.headline: Overall council financial sustainability at extreme risk due to funding withdrawal and cost pressures.
findings.detail: The strategic financial risk (RD-S01) is rated Red 35 unmitigated—the highest category. Central Government funding cuts and lost income combined with rising demand create a perfect storm. The council acknowledges inadequate controls could lead to significant overspend on capital projects, directly impacting reserves and the council's ability to plan cuts.
findings.matters: This is the top-level financial sustainability risk; if realised, it forces deeper cuts and constrains borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: RD-S01 unmitigated rating 35 (Almost Certain 5 × Extreme/Catastrophic 7); mitigated to Amber 12
findings.quote: Failure to maintain the overall financial health of the Council (Central Government Funding and lost income, as well as increasing demand and cost pressures) could result in a lack of long-term financial sustainability. This could impact on reserve levels, quantum of cuts and ability to plan cuts.

findings.headline: Cannot recruit and retain enough qualified social workers in either children's or adults' services.
findings.detail: Both children's (CSCLL-S05) and adults' (IASCS-S02) social care face Almost Certain workforce shortages, with Extreme/Catastrophic impact. The adults' services risk explicitly cites government policy on overseas workers creating an uncontrollable 'cliff edge'. Vacant roles strain existing teams and may compromise service quality and safeguarding.
findings.matters: Staffing shortages in statutory services can force the council into emergency outsourcing at premium cost, or face service failure and regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: CSCLL-S05 and IASCS-S02 both Red 35 unmitigated; likelihood Almost Certain 5, impact Extreme/Catastrophic 7; both mitigated to Red 21
findings.quote: The Government position on overseas skilled workers and dependents may create a 'cliff edge' that the Council cannot influence or control. Roles may remain vacant for some time before successfully being filled, leading to additional strain on existing team members.

findings.headline: Adults' social care funding exposed to uncontrollable national policy changes (National Insurance, National Living Wage).
findings.detail: The council faces almost certain demand for adult social care with extreme/catastrophic consequence, and explicitly cannot control cost drivers set by central government (National Insurance increases, National Living Wage). Forecasting challenges are acknowledged to threaten financial stability.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded, uncontrollable cost escalator in a ringfenced budget; the council has no mitigation levers.
findings.figures: Unmitigated risk rating 35 (IASCS-S01, IASCS-S03); likelihood Almost Certain 5, impact Extreme/Catastrophic 7; IASCS-S03 mitigated only to Amber 9
findings.quote: In some cases, the Council has limited or no opportunity to influence National government decisions regarding changes in policy or taxation which will affect the Council financially (for example, National Insurance and National Living Wage increases). Forecasting challenges may occur, resulting in reduced financial stability.

findings.headline: Children's social care facing uncontrollable cost pressures from rising demand.
findings.detail: The council faces almost certain demand growth for children's social care but insufficient local capacity. Children are being placed outside the borough in high-cost and unregulated arrangements, driving direct budget pressures. The unmitigated risk is rated 28–35 (highest category) even after mitigation.
findings.matters: Unfunded social care demand is a material threat to financial sustainability; costs rise regardless of council action and cannot be capped.
findings.figures: Unmitigated risk rating 28 (CSCLL-S01) and 35 (CSCLL-S03); likelihood Almost Certain 5, impact Extreme/Catastrophic 7; mitigated risk 21
findings.quote: Providing additional years of SEND support has a significant financial impact on the Council, which could reduce available budget for the delivery of other vital services. There is a risk that children live in high cost and / or in unregulated arrangements which drives costs and pressures on Council budgets.

findings.paper_title: RTC - Medium Term Financial Strategy 202627 – 203031 B
findings.headline: Emissions Trading Scheme cost for waste estimated at £2.6m; new unfunded pressure subject to review
